Simulation

A virtual Yeti, ice bottle and gate running the same physics and thermostat as the real cooler. Switch the data source to Simulation to see it on the dashboard.

Inside the cooler

The Stanley hangs upside down over the gate. As the ice melts, meltwater collects at the neck and the ice above it shrinks.
Fuel left– Ice still frozen– Meltwater– Cold flowing in– Heat leaking in– Yeti lid–
Design note: meltwater pools right above the gate. In the real build, use sealed ice packs or a fine drip screen in the neck so water can't drip into the Yeti when the flap opens.

Blue dots are cold air sinking through the gate. Orange dots are room heat getting in through the walls and lid.

AI

Show Claude a medicine or a cold pack, set how long it has to last, and it works out the safest settings. Everything you save is stored on the ESP32, so it stays there when the board is unplugged.

Control the ESP32 from inside Claude

Claude's viewer can't open USB ports. A small helper on your computer holds the port, and this page talks to it through the Claude desktop app.
Not connected
  1. Install Python 3.10 or newer from python.org (tick Add python.exe to PATH). Then in a terminal run py -m pip install mcp pyserial
  2. Save frostgate_bridge.py in your FrostGate folder.
  3. In the Claude desktop app open Settings → Developer → Edit Config, paste the config below and save. If the file already has an mcpServers section, add only the "frostgate" entry inside it.

        

        
    
          
  1. Fully quit Claude (tray icon → Quit) and reopen it.
    2. 
          
  2. Open this artifact in the desktop app and press Claude app at the top. Allow access when Claude asks.

While the bridge runs it holds the COM port. Quit the Claude app before uploading firmware from Arduino IDE.

      

      

        

          
Flash the firmware (once)

          
    
            
  1. In Arduino IDE, install the esp32 board package (Espressif).
    2. 
            
  2. Library Manager: install OneWire, DallasTemperature, ESP32Servo, ArduinoJson (v7).
    3. 
            
  3. Board: ESP32S3 Dev Module. Plugged into the port marked USB? Set USB CDC On Boot: Enabled.
    4. 
            
  4. Open FrostGate.ino, upload, then close the Serial Monitor (only one app can hold the port).
    5. 
            
  5. Open this console in Chrome or Edge, press Connect USB. After that, all pin changes happen here.
    6. 
          

        

        

          
Good to know

          
    
            
  1. One 4.7 kΩ pull-up from the 1-Wire data line to 3.3 V covers every probe on that pin.
    2. 
            
  2. The onboard RGB LED is GPIO 48 on most S3 DevKitC-1 boards and GPIO 38 on v1.1 boards. If it stays dark, try the other.
    3. 
            
  3. Plain LEDs need a 220–330 Ω resistor. A fan needs a logic-level MOSFET and a flyback diode; the GPIO can't power it directly.
    4. 
            
  4. Power a servo from 5 V, not the 3.3 V pin, and join its ground to the ESP32's ground.
    5. 
            
  5. Two ways to connect: Claude app (this page inside the Claude desktop app, through the bridge above) or Connect USB (the downloaded file in Chrome or Edge).
    6.
